title: The cave and the breath
hookLine: the Lord set the soul in the cave of the body and played the breath like music (Anand)

lines: THE RAGI'S LEFT HAND ON THE BELLOWS.
THE SAME IDEA, INSIDE A PERSON.
cards: During kirtan, watch the ragi's left hand. While the right hand plays the keys of the harmonium, the left works the bellows at the back, folding and unfolding, steady, the whole time.
Without that push of air, the keys are just wood. With it, the hall fills with sound. Today's pauri is far older than the harmonium, but it sees the same idea inside every person.

teach.h: GUFAA: THE BODY AS A CAVE.
teach.b: The pauri opens, in paraphrase: the beloved Lord placed the soul inside the cave, and played the instrument of the breath.
The cave, gufaa, is the body: dark, enclosed, hollow, like the caves where people in India have long gone to meditate.
The instrument, vaajaa, is played by pavan, air, breath. So every breath is the Lord playing music in a cave. Then the pauri gets specific.

teach.h: NINE DOORS PLAIN, THE TENTH HIDDEN.
teach.b: In that body, nine doors were made plain to see, and the tenth was kept hidden.
The pauri doesn't list the nine; commentators read them as the body's openings: the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth and the two below. The tenth door, dasvaa duaar, is hidden.
Sikh teachers describe it in different ways; one common reading is an inner opening, not a physical one, the place where a person comes to know the One.

teach.h: THE GURU'S DOOR SHOWS THE TENTH.
teach.b: And the pauri says how it's found: through the Guru's door, with loving faith, some are shown the tenth door. There, it says, are many forms, the Name, the nine treasures, and no one can find the end of them.
It closes on its first line: the Lord placed the soul in the cave and played the breath. Look at this week's order.
The body was asked what it had done, told where its light came from, then the eyes and ears were given their work.
Now, underneath all of it, the breath: the music nobody has to remember to play.

how: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; in the gurdwara, kirtan is commonly sung to the harmonium and tabla, and many Sikhs pair simran, remembering the Name, with the breath.

o: a mountain shrine where hermits pray
the bellows that push air into a harmonium
a cave: the body, where the soul is placed

games.q: the cave pauri — tap the pairs.

s: the pauri says the Lord plays the breath like an instrument
the soul is placed in the cave of the body and the breath is played.
the pauri says all ten of the body's doors are plain to see
nine are made plain; the tenth is kept hidden.
through the tenth door, the pauri says, the end of the Lord's treasures is found
it says no one can find the end of them.

games.q: the pauri says the body has nine doors you can see and a tenth that is hidden. how is the tenth one shown?
o: by holding the breath as long as possible.
through the Guru's door, with loving faith.
it is shown to everyone at birth.
games.why: the pauri says that through the Guru's door, with loving faith, some are shown the tenth door.

practice: Sit still and breathe in through the nose a little slower than usual, listening to the sound it makes, then breathe out and listen to that too: in, out, like the ragi's hand on the bellows.
Don't try to make it beautiful; the pauri says it's already music. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along on one breath.

wordCard.voice: Gufaa, cave. In the Anand, the Lord places the soul in the gufaa of the body and plays the breath like an instrument; nine doors are open, and the tenth is hidden.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gufaa, cave; the Anand's picture of the body, where the soul is placed and the breath is played.

carryVoice: Your line: breath is music. The bellows have kept going all day without being asked. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand, the cave pauri (har jeeo gufaa andar rakh kai vaajaa pavan vajaaiaa), Ang 922
